title: Does Night of the Living Dead (1968) have a poorly executed motif?

commenti.body: I don’t know too much about his political or social/personal reasonings for making night of the living dead, but  I will say I did a bit of a deep dive into Romero for a ‘Art of Pittsburgh’ talk and I do know one of his main reasons he made this movie was that he wanted to tackle the idea of zombies a different way from the way that the 1954 book I Am Legend tackled the genre. Where that one focused more on the global response and effects to a ‘ghoul apocalypse’ Romero wanted to really ground it and focus on the small rural interpersonal response to a zombie apocalypse. I know he intentionally left the political and social commentary vague, but I don’t know if it was for ‘pessimistic outlook’ reasons or more that maybe he made this art piece for one reason, and then the masses react how they do, and now he’s like ‘meh sure it’s whatever you interpret’ . Idk if this adds anything to the argument but felt like I needed to just shoot a fun fact in here lol

I think Romero's follow ups show his attitude toward social ills and anxieties. I don't think he would be against a counterculture movement like the hippies. 


In addition to I am Legend, I found similarities with The Killer Shrews (1959) and Five (1951) in the structure and conflicts. Regarding race, all films feature a black man and he dies in all of them. Five directly deals with a racist character but The Killer Shrews just feels racist in its depiction. All of these stories use an isolated house as a main setting and the tension inside is just as much a threat as outside. 


When it comes to what represents a new generation of ideology, I don't think the zombies can be said to represent it. Like giant shrews or the dead vampires in I am Legend, they just consume. They don't cooperate but unintentionally help each other when they break down windows and doors. 



Because Ben is aligned with the zombies in the eyes of the white men who shoot without thinking straight, the Apocalypse makes us all mindless but the victims above others are the minorities we mainly discriminate against.

>Romero appears to be drawing parallels to hippie communists. Where the humans are divided constantly throughout the film, the zombies are unified. They care not for petty social norms like gender, race, class, nudity, or class. They're a mindless horde of homogeny, all cooperating for a certain goal. This seems like a gross generalization of civil rights movements during the 60's

Wholeheartedly and fundamentally disagree with this take, although I see how it may have merit. This, in a way, implies that Romero created the concept of the zombie. He did indeed employ it, and has some tie to its narrative implications, but most of what you described is simply the "art of the dead." You are presuming that those traits are designed to match a group, culture, and/or opinion which is something that we do out of our own prejudice, and not logic based on the creator and their piece.

The minorities of this film may not all die to zombies, but they are indeed fighting for their lives against them. The zombies in that case, with your logic, would then represent something "outside" the system of racism (the very alive farmers who kill him in the end). So the zombies are... humans which exist outside of society... so they're... anarchists or barbarians or inhuman. I don't think any of this is the case, I'm just trying to level with this style of logic and help you see why it doesn't apply to the movie.

Night of the Living Dead to me feels almost apolitical, but leaves that door open a crack to allow for a purposely vague political interpretation if desired. It has certain qualities in common with other post-apocalyptic science fiction like War of the Worlds, Day of the Triffids, etc. These can also be interpreted politically if desired, though I think they work primarily as imaginative adventure/horror stories where all humans become fugitives. Night of the Living Dead follows this template but adds the cultural DNA of its own time and place, so it makes sense that it feels vaguely political. Personally I view the movie as a great example of imaginative nut-n-bolts low budget filmmaking. It practically invented an entire horror genre and still feels fresh and grimy today.

Romero speaks about his relationship with Richard Matheson's I am Legend a lot. In fact, Romero drawing inspiration from I Am Legend is what prompted me to start drawing these parallels with Night of the Living Dead. For as cool as they are, I think they really don't act as great allegories for racism and the new generation. The characteristics of the vampires in I Am Legend for what we know aren't nice. I feel as though this by diffusion bleeds into Night of the Living Dead. Really both of these stories are pessimistic. The New Order in I Am Legend isn't necessarily better than the human world before it, just different. I think that narrative is driven home clearly. The Legend part of the title even drives home that inverse of how we humans view vampires as legendary monsters, the vampires of the New Order view Neville as their monster of legend. If we are to tie it back to being an allegory for moving away from old society filled with white racists to a new society with black "vampires", remarking both as essentially the same, it leaves a bad taste now doesn't it? Comes off at worst as a bitter white man's last stand before society moving onto an age where white's are not only the minority but wiped out completely. The Great Replacement narrative isn't new but it's still prominent in modern politics and has echoes of this idea. At best, it seems to be an insipid statement about humanity being evil regardless of their values or how they change. For that reason, I hope you see how I'm paralleling it to Night of the Living Dead because George Romero talks about the latter idea often when interviewed about what he felt the meaning of his film was. I'll link what I found in interviews in my post as an edit. I should've done so to begin with but was being a bit lazy.

I don't see how it does. You can use a concept well established with a new take to view it through. I don't believe the film itself does this but I'm referring to George's specific comment's about what he feels the film means. I neglected to link those interviews but the parallels to racism in the film have been analyzed and discussed to death by this point and people seem to agree that even though George Romero has admitted on many occasions that the racial allegory wasn't intentional, it happened to fit in the film perfectly nonetheless, so why can't this, especially when there is context from the creator to support it? I'll be linking context in an edited portion of my original post so maybe my ideas will be more clear afterwards.

The living humans locked in the farm house have a lot of advantages over the zombies, or ghouls, but their downfall results from the disagreements and social divisions within the house. This is contrasted with the zombie horde which, as you stated, are united with no regard to race, class, or gender. In the end Ben is taken down by other humans who don't see him as human. 

I would interpret the moral lesson of the film is about our inability to work together and see our shared humanity.

I'm genuinely confused what the point of all this is. 

If it was all unintentional, then the film didn't fail at portraying its motifs... him saying the message is "hey can't we all just get along" is incredibly well portrayed in the movie... in that this is a living vs dead film. He took a concept, used horror as an allegory, and showed us that we all die anyways. We are the same. The movie opens with someone instigating Barbara, we're needlessly attack one other, we turn into zombies. Only those who find community survive.

It seems like his idea was quite simple. And in that, the film was quite simple. 

And the racial allegory is denied by the director and theorized by viewers, and likely evident of the thinking and culture of the time just by happenstance.

Well, you've kinda answered your own question. No, it accomplished what Romero intended it to. He intended it to be a commentary on "the young devouring the old". Abandoning their old ideals and morals for an entirely different set. It fits well because you can either watch it with these in mind or not and enjoy the film all the same.

>Abandoning their old ideals and morals for an entirely different set.



Except I don't think he meant this at all because then it would mean he was specifically referring to hippie communists but Romero was more vague than that. He was speaking about how these people are entranced in ideology like zombies, attacking the normal people and causing the breakdown of society.



>It fits well because you can either watch it with these in mind or not and enjoy the film all the same.



Ultimately, it's art and as long as you interpret it well, it can mean anything you want. Like the racism allegory with Ben's character.

If it was all unintentional, then the film didn't fail at portraying its motifs... him saying the message is "hey can't we all just get along" is incredibly well portrayed in the movie... in that this is a living vs dead film.

I agree actually. I don't think that is the motif I'm focused on though. I was more concerned with his characterization of the zombies and what they represent to humans. Personally, I prefer to think of them as a natural disaster because it perfectly aligns with the express theme of human dysfunction that he lays out, which is a theme I can get behind. However, the comments made me think it was directed towards a specific group but it wasn't unless you consider people with "ideology" a group. I think it's a vapid statement to make but for what he intended to do, he succeeded. My question was poorly worded. I meant to say this motif seems in poor taste or ignorant, which he admitted later that he was ignorant to racial and gender issues in an interview.   
  
 [https://youtu.be/uCpJKakWVRc?si=eVQSeJLyKXfXbaV6&t=1502](https://youtu.be/uCpJKakWVRc?si=eVQSeJLyKXfXbaV6&t=1502)

There are so many interpretations people have dug into from Night of the Living Dead beyond the groupthink, subversions of social order and nature of humanity themes Romero express himself. Atomic fear, civil rights, capitalism and conformity to name a few. Not all of which I agree with but I can see. 

>However this does make me want to hear your take on Texas Chainsaw (the most vegan film I've ever seen)

I love Texas Chainsaw Massacre but I only have vague concepts of what it can mean. I have yet to sit back and think on it but I know there is a lot to talk about.

Just so you know hippie culture wasn't inherently communist. There were a lot of hippies who were communist but you didn't have to be a communist to be a hippie or vice versa. Only saying because I noticed that you've mentioned this a lot in other comments. It's kinda confusing the point you are trying to make. 

I think his point was much simpler than you are thinking it was. It wasn't about communism. If we're going with the  generational divide angle, which I must admit I'd not thought of until I read your sources, then it is just about old ideas being "devoured" and replaced by new ones. The risks of this and how this can harm social cohesion. It can be applied to any generation that inspires huge social change, including our own. He's basically saying slow down and think before you forsake everything your parents told you. 

Weirdly enough, since the racism angle was the major thing everyone remembers (Ben's murder at the end), I always thought this was the main point. I was surprised to hear this was unintended.

>Just so you know hippie culture wasn't inherently communist. There were a lot of hippies who were communist but you didn't have to be a communist to be a hippie or vice versa. Only saying because I noticed that you've mentioned this a lot in other comments. It's kinda confusing the point you are trying to make. 

I'm aware I was more referencing the idea of hippies being viewed communists by people in that era.

>I think his point was much simpler than you are thinking it was. It wasn't about communism. If we're going with the generational divide angle, which I must admit I'd not thought of until I read your sources, then it is just about old ideas being "devoured" and replaced by new ones. The risks of this and how this can harm social cohesion. It can be applied to any generation that inspires huge social change, including our own. He's basically saying slow down and think before you forsake everything your parents told you. 

Romero is definitely making a negative statement on groupthink, human nature, and social order. I don't think his zombie metaphor works very well though.

>Weirdly enough, since the racism angle was the major thing everyone remembers (Ben's murder at the end), I always thought this was the main point. I was surprised to hear this was unintended.

It is suprising to hear because I don't believe the film would be so enduring if Ben was anything but a black man. There are a lot of happy accidents that just make the film racial, despite Romero's desire to be starkly apolitical.

>The living humans locked in the farm house have a lot of advantages over the zombies, or ghouls, but their downfall results from the disagreements and social divisions within the house.

I see this theme visibly. I was more focused on what the Zombies themselves represent because of how Romero characterized them.

>In the end Ben is taken down by other humans who don't see him as human. 

Are you saying this because he is black? Or is it because they genuinely thought he was a zombie?

>I would interpret the moral lesson of the film is about our inability to work together and see our shared humanity.

That is definitely an intention by Romero. I agree.

I mean, if you were to look through the lense that the zombies are supposed to represent the hippie generation devouring everything, then this film is pretty prophetic, then given how Boomers (aka the Hippies) grew up with the greatest generational privilage and *have* consumed everything in their path. Old generation and new. Looking around at the slow rot that has happened over the 40 or so years they have been running things it's not unlike a slow shambling zombie. That's my modernest take on that intention now.

That said, with some movies there can be a delinitation between intent and interpretation. Or to put it another way, the idea of the mind sometimes gets translated to film in an unexpected way. No, Romero didn't intend a lot of the take aways people got from his films -- and you can really give him credit for admitting that outright -- but art always is subjective. I think we forget that film is like any other art form in that what it is to people can vary differently, even netween artist and audience. Sometimes we are too busy trying to try and understand the artists intention rather than what it means to the viewer. The intent is anectdotal, I think. It's good to know, but it's not the "right" way to interpret a film.

There are wrong wats to interpret a film, but that's usually the type of person who doesn't understand story telling to begin with. Like people who claim to be life long fans of Star Trek who decry the new series as being "woke", for instance. Just a fundimental lack of critical though about a piece of art.

>Boomers (aka the Hippies)

It's a bit disingenious to classify Boomers as Hippies, their was a huge culture war and generational divide. I don't think the Hippies are the same people that are doing what you described.

Like people who claim to be life long fans of Star Trek who decry the new series as being "woke", for instance. Just a fundimental lack of critical though about a piece of art.

I agree fully however I always try to see what the creator intended, if they speak on the matter at all. I take my own interpretations still because he can't stop that as long as it is sensible and fits within a narrative.

The Baby Boom Generation applies to everyone born between 1946 and 1964. So the term does apply. Granted everyone of that age wasn't a hippie but retrospectively that was the movement that defined that generation. But agreed to disagree. It's neither here nor there to me, really.

For sure, understanding what they intended vs how its interpreted is important in understanding the art.
My personal feeling is that Romero had a great skill for creating movies which felt richly laden with metaphor, but I don’t think he always had a clear idea himself of what the metaphors meant..
